name: Question 3
worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=2$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{3x+1}-\sqrt{7}} & =\frac{2-2}{\sqrt{3(2)+1}-\sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{2-2}{\sqrt{7}-\sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{3x+1}-\sqrt{7}} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{(\sqrt{3x+1}-\sqrt{7})(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{(\sqrt{3x+1})^{2}-(\sqrt{7})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{3x+1-7} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{3x-6} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{3(x-2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3(2)+1}+\sqrt{7}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{7}}{3} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{7}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at x=2, we get an indeterminate form: limx→2x−23x+1−7=2−23(2)+1−7=2−27−7=00

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get limx→2x−23x+1−7=limx→2(x−2)(3x+1+7)(3x+1−7)(3x+1+7)=limx→2(x−2)(3x+1+7)(3x+1)2−(7)2=limx→2(x−2)(3x+1+7)3x+1−7=limx→2(x−2)(3x+1+7)3x−6=limx→2(x−2)(3x+1+7)3(x−2)=limx→23x+1+73=3(2)+1+73=7+73=273.
